svg.title: A fully meshed IPsec network still lets one compromised PC reach every site
svg.desc: Left: three sites joined in a full IPsec mesh. A compromised PC behind site A opens an ordinary TCP session to a file share in site B and to a database in site C. Every packet is encrypted, every peer is authenticated, and the firewall sees only tunnel endpoints, so nothing in the path has a reason to object. Right: what IPsec does give - confidentiality on the wire, peer authentication, integrity, replay protection. What it does not give - authorization of the user, content inspection, control of lateral movement, logging of which internal host talked to which, or any awareness that the endpoint is already owned. A footer states that encryption answers cannot-see, access control answers cannot-get-in, and the two are frequently confused in the same design paragraph.
svg.text: "We have IPsec everywhere" answers a question nobody in the incident call is asking
The tunnel is doing exactly what it was designed to do while the breach spreads through it.
FULL MESH, ALL TUNNELS UP, ALL PEERS AUTHENTICATED
Site A
HQ / data centre
Site B
file share
Site C
database
IPsec
IPsec
IPsec
owned PC
(user credentials)
The session from the owned PC is an ordinary TCP
connection. It gets a tunnel, an authenticated peer
and confidentiality - all of which are true and
all of which are irrelevant to stopping it.
The path sees tunnel endpoints, never hosts.
No control point has a reason to object.
WHAT ENCRYPTION DOES GIVE
confidentiality on the wire
peer authentication at tunnel setup
integrity and replay protection
a safe path across an untrusted network
all four are about the transport, not the person
and none of them survive "the endpoint is owned"
WHAT IT DOES NOT GIVE
authorization: may this user reach that host
content inspection: what is inside the tunnel
lateral movement control: A to B to C chaining
per-host logging: which internal pair talked
endpoint health: is the sender already owned
"cannot see" is solved. "cannot get in" is not.
Test before deployment: name the control that answers "this authenticated user must not reach that server". If the answer is "the VPN", there is no control.
